newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala signs pact ending 36-year guerrilla war.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala signs pact ending 36-year guerrilla war.

text.p: Guatemala's government and Marxist rebels signed a historic treaty on Sunday ending one of Latin America's longest-running guerrilla wars, and they pledged a brighter future after decades of brutality.

In a glittering ceremony in the courtyard of the National Palace, leaders of the four main factions of the Guatemalan National Liberation Unit (URNG) rebels and government peace negotiatiors signed the agreement, which formally put an end to a 36-year conflict in which 140,000 people died.

"This day of justifiable and genuine national celebration is the most transcendental and significant in the history of our country in the last 50 years," veteran URNG commander Ricardo Ramirez de Leon said in a speech hailing the treaty.
The accord was signed by President Alvaro Arzu and the leaders of other Latin American countries and Spain in the presence of hundreds of other international dignitaries.

Addressing them in a sombre suit and reading glasses, the rebel leader -- who dropped his nom de guerre, Rolando Moran, for the ceremony -- defended the decision to take up arms decades ago because of the collapse of democracy.
But his message, like that of chief government negotiator Gustavo Porras, was one of reconciliation and forgiveness in a country once torn apart by fratricide.
"We can and we must create a better country, and this is the opportunity. Peace will only be what we make it," Porras said.

Boutros Boutros-Ghali, outgoing secretary-general of the United Nations, which brokered the negotiations, also signed the accord and urged the world not to turn its back on the impoverished country now that it had finished the war.

The treaty cuts by a third the strength of the 43,000-person army, which for almost 30 years up to 1986 ruled the country with an iron fist and was responsible for atrocities that gave Guatemala the worst human rights record in Latin America.
It will lead to the disbanding of the URNG fighters, whose numbers have shrunk to 1,700 but who still live under arms in remote mountain and jungle regions observing a ceasefire.

It also strengthens the rights of the majority Indian population, who have been the main victims of the conflict, suffering massacres, disappearances and a brutal racism that is still far from eroded.
But carrying the agreement through will require international financial backing estimated as high as $2.3 billion. Arzu's government has recently gone the rounds cap in hand for support.
"The international community must not turn its attention away, especially in the critical early stages of implementation," Boutros-Ghali, who leaves office at midnight on Tuesday, said.
Outside the palace, tens of thousands of Guatemalans cheered as they watched the signing ceremony on giant video screens. Fireworks exploded over the city centre.
The crowds included jubilant supporters of the URNG, who earlier marched on the central plaza freely chanting support for the rebel cause for the first time in their lives.
